processing: Mostly orthodox Darjeeling black tea: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, with oxidation lighter in spring than in summer. The division also sells clonal, oolong and Moonshine-style lots.
harvest_season: Spring first flush and autumn flush are the Liza Hill lots usually seen for sale; the wider garden is known for its second flush from around May to June.
appearance_dry: Twisted leaf in mixed green, olive and brown, lighter in first flush lots and darker in autumn, as is usual in Darjeeling.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in first flush, deepening to amber in autumn lots.
appearance_wet: Soft, mixed green and copper leaf, greener in spring.
taste_profile: Little is recorded for this division alone. Expect what is typical of organic Darjeeling: floral and brisk in spring, rounder and more fruity in later flushes.

brewing.notes: Brewed Western-style. Drop to about 85 C for delicate first flush lots and shorten the steep if it turns sharp.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush, with the name of the lot on the label: First Flush 2024, Autumn Flush 2023 and so on. Clonal, Moonshine and oolong lots appear as small limited editions. As with other Darjeeling, buy the most recent harvest and drink spring lots within a year or two.
description:
Liza Hill is a section of the Risheehat garden (also spelled Rishihat) in eastern Darjeeling, about 14 km from the town. It once ran as a separate estate with its own factory, and the name survives on lots sold from this part of the garden.

The tea here is certified organic and mostly made in the orthodox Darjeeling way. The same division also turns out clonal grades, oolong and limited Moonshine lots, so the name on the bag tells you the place, not the style.

Little has been written about how Liza Hill differs in the cup from the rest of Risheehat. Treat it as you would any organic Darjeeling: a spring lot is floral and brisk and suffers from boiling water, while an autumn lot takes more heat and gets rounder.

When buying, look for the year, the flush and the grade or lot name. Comparing a Liza Hill lot with a plain Risheehat one from the same season is the simplest way to judge whether the name means anything to you.
history:
The wider garden was started by the British in the 1900s under the name Tshering Bagan, and was later renamed Risheehat, explained locally as home of the sages. Jay Shree Tea, part of the B. K. Birla Group, acquired it in 1955.

Liza Hill was a separate estate with its own factory until 1963 and later became a division of Risheehat. Little else is documented about its early years.
